claims.text: Introducing oxygen-containing defects into a carbon support shifts the d-band center of supported Pt nanoparticles.
Shifting the Pt d-band center optimizes the adsorption energies of oxygen intermediates in ORR.
Optimizing oxygen-intermediate adsorption through support defects enhances ORR activity.
Oxygen defects in the carbon support enhance the durability of supported Pt nanoparticles.
Pt nanoparticles on pristine carbon with minimal oxygen defects constitute the baseline material.
The controlled comparison should introduce oxygen functionalization while holding Pt nanoparticle size and dispersion constant.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to acidic ORR operation at approximately 60–80°C.
The Pt–support interface is the structural mediator through which oxygen defects modulate Pt electronic structure.
Electronic modulation of Pt changes the binding energies of key ORR oxygen intermediates.
Adjusted intermediate binding energies improve charge-transfer kinetics.
Improved charge-transfer kinetics lower ORR overpotential.
Electronic modulation caused by oxygen defects reduces catalyst degradation.
Defect-rich oxygen-functionalized supports will produce a measurable Pt d-band-center shift relative to pristine supports.
Defect-rich oxygen-functionalized supports will produce lower ORR overpotentials than pristine supports.
Defect-rich oxygen-functionalized supports will degrade more slowly than pristine supports.
Supported Pt nanoparticles are an established carbon-supported ORR catalyst architecture with long-term activity and electrochemical-surface-area losses.
Changing pH, temperature, or defect density may change the hypothesized behavior.
Unintended changes in Pt nanoparticle morphology could confound attribution of performance changes to electronic modulation.
